description: TT Media Server (Python) - request latency, pipeline stages, image-generation stage breakdown (denoising / VAE decode / conditioning), multihost video-gen breakdown, and per-process infrastructure. Transient asset; sunsets with the Python server (~4 months).

panels.description: Total HTTP requests/sec hitting the FastAPI server (auto-instrumented).
panels.title: Request Rate

panels.description: Generation jobs currently being processed by the model service (post-queue, pre-response). Reflects true model concurrency, unlike the HTTP in-flight gauge which only sees the ~2ms queue-and-202 handler.
panels.title: Jobs In Flight (model)

panels.description: 5xx error ratio over the last 5m. Alert threshold: 5%.
panels.title: Error Rate (5xx)

panels.description: End-to-end p99 request latency (FastAPI auto-instrumented).
panels.title: HTTP p99 Latency

panels.description: p50/p95/p99 of total request duration, grouped by model_type. Filter via the $model_type variable to focus on a single runner (e.g. sp_runner for video gen).
panels.title: End-to-End Latency Quantiles

panels.description: Successful requests/sec per model_type from the custom telemetry counter.
panels.title: Requests / sec per model_type
Pipeline Stages (where time is spent inside a request)

panels.description: p95 latency of each pipeline stage stacked. Lets you see which stage dominates request time.
panels.title: Pipeline Stage p95 (stacked)

panels.description: Finished video generations per minute across all outcomes (success, failure, cancelled). Video is slow work, so per-minute reads better than per-second.
panels.title: Generations / min

panels.description: Share of finished generations that produced a video over the last 1h. Failures are timeouts and runner/peer errors, not HTTP 4xx. Cancelled generations are excluded from both sides of the ratio — /cancel traffic is a client action, not a reliability signal. Empty (not 0% or 100%) when no success/failure completed in the window, including non-video model_type filters.
panels.title: Success Rate

panels.description: Video generations currently being processed, summed across request types. Narrower than Jobs In Flight, which counts every model_type.
panels.title: Generations In Flight

panels.description: 95th-percentile wall-clock time for a successful generation: queue wait + inference + mp4 encode.
panels.title: Generation p95

panels.description: Wall-clock seconds spent per second of playable video. 1.0 = realtime; 100 = a 5s clip took ~8 minutes. Resolution-independent, so it is the one number to compare pipelines with.
panels.title: Realtime Factor p95

panels.description: Seconds since the last successful generation while idle. 0 while video_generations_in_progress > 0 so a 20-minute job does not go yellow at 15 minutes. Rising without bound after in-flight drops to 0 means the pipeline stopped producing — a wedged runner that never returns an error.
panels.title: Since Last Success

panels.description: Finished generations per minute split by t2v vs i2v and outcome. The request type is derived from the payload (presence of image_prompts), so /i2v and /i2v/upload share a series.
panels.title: Generation rate by type / status

panels.description: End-to-end generation time for successful requests, by type. Failures are excluded on purpose — a timeout says nothing about how long the pipeline takes when it works. Plot status="failure" separately to see time-to-failure.
panels.title: Generation latency quantiles (success)

panels.description: Frames produced per wall-clock second within a single generation, by resolution. This is the per-request speed, not fleet throughput.
panels.title: Frame throughput per generation

panels.description: Wall-clock seconds per diffusion step (generation time / steps requested), by resolution. Success-only: a timed-out request never ran its steps.
panels.title: Mean denoise step latency

panels.description: Wall seconds per second of playable video, by resolution. Flat under load = the pipeline is keeping up; rising = contention or a straggler host.
panels.title: Realtime factor distribution

panels.description: Aggregate output rate across all in-flight generations: frames, denoise steps, and seconds of playable video produced per second. Steps/sec is the one to watch when comparing runner builds.
panels.title: Work produced per second (fleet)

panels.description: width x height x frames per wall-clock second, by resolution. Lets a 480p run and a 720p run be compared on equal terms — frames/sec cannot.
panels.title: Pixel throughput per generation

panels.description: Size of the mp4 handed back to the client. A sudden drop with steady frame counts usually means a degraded or truncated encode.
panels.title: Output mp4 size

panels.description: ffmpeg encode latency and frames/sec, recorded where the encode runs (in-process runners and CPU postprocessing workers). A multihost SP_RUNNER deployment encodes inside its external peer, which serves no /metrics, so these series are absent there by design.
panels.title: MP4 encode cost

panels.description: What clients are asking for: mean num_inference_steps per request and mean image_prompts count on I2V. A shift here explains a latency shift that is not a regression.
panels.title: Steps requested vs I2V conditioning images

panels.description: Lifetime totals since server start, by request type. Frames and video-seconds are success-only; the generation count includes failures.
panels.title: Video totals by request type

panels.description: Frames the VAE converts from latents to pixels per second of VAE-busy time - its intrinsic decode rate, independent of how often it runs. Deliberately not rate(frames_total): that is fleet output rate, it tracks whatever the slowest stage is, and tt_media_server_video_frames_generated_total already reports it. No data (not zero) when nothing decoded in the window. Emitted by the Wan2.2 family and Mochi; the Prodia distills, LTX and MiniMax-H3 expose no VAE span.
panels.title: VAE Throughput (frames/VAE-s)

panels.description: Megapixels the VAE converts per second of VAE-busy time. Resolution-independent view of reconstruction capacity - frames alone make a 480p model look faster than a 720p one at equal silicon cost. Same busy-time normalisation as the frames panel.
panels.title: VAE Throughput (MP/VAE-s)

panels.description: VAE decode rate per output resolution, per second of VAE-busy time. Read it with the Denoise vs VAE split: this panel says how fast reconstruction is, that one says how much of the device time it is eating. A resolution whose rate here falls while its pixel count is unchanged is a real regression, not a traffic change - busy-time normalisation removes the load signal.
panels.title: VAE decode rate by resolution (per VAE-busy second)

panels.description: Time to decode one video's latents to pixels, p50 and p95, per resolution and device. One observation is a whole video, not a frame - divide by the frame count to reason per frame. Do not compare Wan against Mochi here: Wan's span includes the host readback, Mochi's instead includes a device remesh and excludes the PIL conversion. A resolution="unknown" series means the produced frames could not be probed: its latency is still valid, its throughput is not recorded at all.
panels.title: rate(tt_media_server_video_vae_decode_duration_seconds_sum{service=~"$service",model_type=~"$model_type",device_id=~"$device_id"}[5m]) decode latency p50 / p95

panels.description: How the measured device time splits between the sampling loop and the decode. Denoising falling as a share while frames/s stays flat is the rate(tt_media_server_video_vae_decode_duration_seconds_sum{service=~"$service",model_type=~"$model_type",device_id=~"$device_id"}[5m]) becoming the limiter. Only these two stages are measured - text encoding and latent preparation are not - so this is the split between them, not of the whole request, and it always sums to 100%.
panels.title: Denoise vs rate(tt_media_server_video_vae_decode_duration_seconds_sum{service=~"$service",model_type=~"$model_type",device_id=~"$device_id"}[5m]) time split

panels.description: Completed denoising steps per second across all image models. This is the core generation capacity number: it moves with resolution, step count and batching.
panels.title: Denoising Throughput (steps/s)

panels.description: Images per second converted from latents to pixels by the VAE. Compare against denoising throughput: if this is the lower number, reconstruction is the limiter, not denoising.
panels.title: VAE Decode (images/s)

panels.description: Megapixels per second out of the VAE. Resolution-independent view of reconstruction capacity - images/s alone makes a 512x512 model look faster than a 1024x1024 one at equal silicon cost.
panels.title: VAE Decode (megapixels/s)

panels.description: Conditioning encode time as a share of total engine time. High values mean prompt encoding - not denoising - dominates, which is the usual signature of short/low-step image requests.
panels.title: Conditioning % of Engine Time

panels.description: Denoising steps/s split by resolution and batch size. Doubling resolution should cut steps/s; batching should raise it. If batching does not raise it, the batch is not being formed.
panels.title: Denoising steps/s by resolution & batch

panels.description: Denoising steps/s split by device and sampler. Divergence between devices running the same model and sampler is a per-host problem; divergence between samplers is expected.
panels.title: Denoising steps/s by device & sampler

panels.description: Per-step denoising latency, p50 and p99, by resolution and batch. The reciprocal of p50 is the per-device step rate; a widening p50-p99 gap means some steps are stalling. Only the tt_dit models (SD3.5, Flux, Motif, Qwen-Image) report per-step timings; SDXL and Z-Image-Turbo report only a loop total, so they are absent here by design - use the denoise_duration_seconds panels for those.
panels.title: Denoising step latency p50 / p99

panels.description: Heatmap of per-step denoising latency. Each row is a bucket; intensity = count. Shows bimodal step timing (e.g. first step paying a compile or cache cost) that quantiles hide. Only the tt_dit models (SD3.5, Flux, Motif, Qwen-Image) report per-step timings; SDXL and Z-Image-Turbo report only a loop total, so "No data" here means the runner cannot report it, not that the metric is broken.
panels.title: Denoising step latency heatmap

panels.description: VAE decode throughput per resolution and batch, in images/s and megapixels/s. Flat images/s while denoising steps/s climbs means the VAE has become the bottleneck.
panels.title: VAE decode throughput (images/s & MP/s)

panels.description: VAE decode latency p50/p99 per resolution and batch. Rising with batch means the decode is not amortising across the batch.
panels.title: VAE decode latency p50 / p99

panels.description: Conditioning encode time per request, p50 and p99, in milliseconds. 'all' is the pipeline-level encoder span; clip / t5 / qwen / image are nested inside it, so do not add them to 'all'.
panels.title: Conditioning encoder time p50 / p99 (ms)

panels.description: Conditioning encode time as a percent of engine time, per model. Climbing here on short requests is the signal that prompt encoding, not generation, is what the user is waiting for.
panels.title: Conditioning share of engine time (%)

panels.description: Where engine time goes: conditioning vs denoising vs VAE decode, as a percent of total engine time. Whichever band is widest is the thing to optimise. Bands will not sum to 100% on runners that cannot report every stage (Z-Image-Turbo reports only the total).
panels.title: Engine time split: conditioning vs denoising vs VAE decode (%)

panels.description: Model inference p95 broken down by device_id. For sp_runner (multihost video) each host emits its own time series via TT_VISIBLE_DEVICES. Diverging lines = a slow host (straggler).
panels.title: Inference p95 by device_id

panels.description: Successful model inferences per second per device_id. Tells you how throughput is distributed across hosts.
panels.title: Inferences/sec by device_id (success only)

panels.description: Heatmap of model inference latency. Each row is a latency bucket; intensity = count. Reveals bimodal distributions and tail latency growth that quantiles can hide.
panels.title: Inference Latency Heatmap

panels.description: Inference success vs failure rate per device_id. A device with rising failures while others are healthy is a host issue, not a model issue.
panels.title: Inference success vs failure by device_id

panels.description: Cross-host inference p95 skew: max(device_id) - min(device_id). Spikes here mean one host is much slower than the others (straggler detection for multihost video gen).

targets.expr: max(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (device_id, le) (rate(tt_media_server_model_inference_duration_seconds_bucket{service=~"$service",model_type=~"$model_type",device_id=~"$device_id"}[5m])))) - min(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (device_id, le) (rate(tt_media_server_model_inference_duration_seconds_bucket{service=~"$service",model_type=~"$model_type",device_id=~"$device_id"}[5m]))))

panels.title: Cross-host p95 skew (straggler detector)

panels.description: Device warmup p95 per device_id. Warmup happens once at startup; long warmup on a single device usually means a slow weight load on that host.
panels.title: Device warmup p95 per device

panels.description: Cumulative device warmup attempts split by status. Persistent failures here block a host from accepting traffic.
panels.title: Warmup totals by device / status

panels.description: Cumulative model load operations split by status. Should stay flat after startup; spikes mean reloads.
panels.title: Model load totals by device / status

panels.description: Result download success vs failure rate. Failures here usually mean object store / network problems, not model problems.
panels.title: Download result rate (success / failure)

panels.description: Result download p95 duration per model_type.
panels.title: Download result p95 duration

panels.description: CPU % consumed by Python tt-media-server processes (uvicorn parent + workers). Sourced from process-exporter group `tt_media_server_python` (see process-exporter.yml).
panels.title: CPU % (Python processes)

panels.description: Resident set size in MB across all Python tt-media-server processes.
panels.title: Memory RSS (MB)

panels.description: Total threads across Python tt-media-server processes.
panels.title: Threads

panels.description: Open file descriptors. Steady growth = leak suspect.
panels.title: Open file descriptors

panels.description: Number of distinct uvicorn / Python worker processes. Verifies your worker fan-out matches the configured count.
panels.title: Process count

panels.description: Major + minor page faults / sec. Sustained majors = thrashing or memory-mapped IO pressure.
panels.title: Page faults / sec

panels.description: System info reported by the server at startup (version, environment, device_mesh_shape, model_runner).
panels.title: Server info

panels.description: Time from chunk hand-off to the first emitted item. Bundles log-mel extraction (~2ms, constant because Whisper pads every chunk to a 30s frame), the encoder pass and the first decode step: tt-metal's WhisperGenerator fuses all three, so they cannot be separated. Unaffected by consumer backpressure.
panels.title: Chunk First-Item Latency Heatmap

panels.description: Wall time to transcribe one chunk end to end. The streaming loop yields to its consumer inside this span, so a slow client inflates this without inflating the first-item metric.
panels.title: Chunk Processing Latency Heatmap

panels.description: Quantiles of both per-chunk spans. First-item is contained in processing by construction, so the first-item lines should always sit below their processing counterparts.
panels.title: Per-Chunk Latency Quantiles

panels.description: Mean seconds per chunk, derived from _sum / _count rather than quantiles, alongside chunk fan-out. Fan-out is the multiplier that makes per-chunk cost matter: every chunk pays a full 30s-frame encoder pass regardless of how short it is, so a heavily diarized request does many times the encoder work of the same audio in fewer chunks.
panels.title: Mean Cost per Chunk and Chunk Fan-out

panels.description: Cumulative observation count at or below each bucket boundary over the selected range. Buckets are cumulative, so the smallest `le` with a non-zero count is the real lower bound of the distribution: everything below it is wasted resolution and the floor can be raised to it.
panels.title: First-Item Bucket Occupancy (set the floor from this)

panels.description: Cumulative observation count at or below each bucket boundary over the selected range. Read the top boundary the same way: if the largest finite bucket already holds every observation, the ceiling can be lowered.
panels.title: Processing Bucket Occupancy (set the floor from this)
ASR Stage Throughput (feature extraction and encoder)

panels.description:
Recorded by the ASR runner only; empty for other model types. Also empty until tt-metal #53717 (PerfMetrics) is in the pinned tt-metal build: the runner probes for it at import and leaves these counters untouched when it is absent, so an empty row here means the dependency has not landed yet, not that the server is idle. Cross-check with the VAD and Input Preparation rows below, which do not depend on it. Audio seconds each stage converts per second **spent inside that stage** — the stage's own capacity, not the server's ingest rate. The denominator is stage-busy time, not wall-clock time, so this does NOT tell you whether the fleet keeps pace with live audio: an encoder busy 10% of the time reads ten times the real-time factor. Use `Ingest Rate` for the keeps-pace question and read this as headroom.

Feature extraction is the preprocessing ceiling and normally sits well above the encoder — convergence means preprocessing has become the limit. The combined line is audio seconds over extraction plus encoder time.

Capacity, not utilisation: short chunks are padded to the 30s frame, so both stages cost the same per chunk whatever its length and this falls with chunk length. A drop can mean fan-out rose, not that the device slowed — read against Chunk Fan-out above.
panels.title: Stage Capacity (audio seconds per stage-busy second)

panels.description:
Audio seconds per encoder-busy second, broken down. Batch: a larger batch amortises one encoder pass over more audio, so this should rise with it — a flat line means batching buys nothing. Device: divergence on the same model is the fleet-capacity signal. Both exclude the trace-capture call.

Same stage-busy denominator as Stage Capacity, so these are per-device capacity figures and are independent of how loaded the device is.
panels.title: Encoder Throughput by Batch and Device

panels.description: Per-batch wall time in each stage. Extraction is host CPU over fixed-size frames, so it should be near-flat — a rising p95 points at host contention, not the model. The encoder spans device preprocessing, the encoder stack and the synchronize.
panels.title: Stage Latency Quantiles

panels.description:
Mean encoder time by trace_hit. trace_hit="false" is the trace-capture call: it runs the encoder twice, so the per-stage lines filter it out. Two exceptions include it deliberately, because feature extraction carries no trace_hit label and a one-sided filter would divide mismatched sets: Stage Capacity's combined line and Ingest Rate. Kept visible for its rate — a steady stream of captures means the batch bucket keeps changing and traces are thrown away rather than replayed.

Expect this to be flat after startup: the capture counter freezes once every batch bucket has a trace, so rate() over it goes to zero and target A's trace_hit="false" series drops out.
panels.title: Trace-Capture Overhead (excluded from the panels above)

panels.description:
Audio seconds ingested per wall-clock second — the real-time factor, and the only panel in this row that answers "can the fleet keep pace with live audio?". Above 1.0 the server consumes audio faster than real time; below 1.0 a live stream falls behind and the backlog grows.

This is the bare numerator of Stage Capacity, with no stage-busy denominator, so it moves with offered load as well as device speed: a low value on an idle server means nothing was submitted, not that the encoder is slow. Read it against Stage Capacity — capacity high but ingest below 1.0 means the front end has headroom and the bottleneck is elsewhere.

Sourced from the feature-extraction counter, which carries no trace_hit label, so trace-capture batches are included.
panels.title: Ingest Rate (audio seconds/s, 1.0 = real time)

panels.description:
Cumulative count at or below each bucket boundary, both stages joined on `le`. The smallest `le` with a non-zero count is the real lower bound — everything below is wasted resolution; if the largest finite bucket holds everything, the ceiling can come down. Re-read after any change to chunk length or device count.

`le` is converted to a number before sorting: as the raw string label it sorts lexicographically, which puts `+Inf` first and `10.0` ahead of `2.5` and makes the "smallest non-zero" reading above wrong. `+Inf` does not parse and sorts last.
panels.title: Stage Duration Bucket Occupancy (set the buckets from this)

panels.description:
Feature-extraction capacity split by the operating point the audio was submitted at. `sample_rate` and `channels` are the source values read off the container header, not the array the extractor sees — audio_manager downmixes to mono and resamples to 16 kHz before the runner is reached, so these are the only record of what arrived.

`unknown` means the decode path normalised the source away before it could be read: ffmpeg is invoked with `-ar/-ac`, so every non-WAV format lands here until an ffprobe pass is added. `mixed` means a batch's items disagreed and the batch was credited under neither.

A high-rate or multi-channel source costs more to decode but not more to extract — the array is mono 16 kHz by then — so a split here points at the decode stage, not the extractor.
panels.title: Feature Extraction Capacity by Source Rate, Channels and Batch

panels.description: Wall time to find speech and endpoint boundaries, per request. VAD gates when inference starts, so this is pure added latency ahead of the encoder — compare it against Chunk First-Item Latency to see which dominates. Quantiles cover successful runs only; a timeout shows up as delay under outcome="failed", not as a non-event.
panels.title: VAD Latency

panels.description: CPU consumed by the VAD worker process divided by its wall time — cores in use, not the caller's clock. Above 1.0 the model went multi-threaded; well below 1.0 with a high latency means the worker was waiting, not computing. Mean CPU seconds per request is the number to multiply by request rate when sizing host cores.
panels.title: VAD CPU Utilisation

panels.description: Speech segments returned per request. This is the endpointing-health signal a duration alone will not show: a collapse toward 1 means VAD stopped splitting and the whole request becomes one long chunk, a jump into the hundreds means it is fragmenting and every fragment pays a full encoder frame. Read against Chunk Fan-out above, which is what these segments merge into.
panels.title: VAD Segments per Request

panels.description: Share of VAD calls that returned nothing, against the call rate. A failure is not a dropped request — the caller falls back to one segment spanning the whole audio, so the cost lands downstream as one oversized chunk. Any sustained non-zero share means the audio venv worker is timing out or respawning.
panels.title: VAD Failure Share

panels.description: Time to base64-decode, container-decode, resample and length-check submitted audio, before VAD sees it. Split by container: mp3 carries a real decode cost that wav does not, so a shift in the format mix moves this without anything regressing. Observed on success only — rejected uploads (unknown header, oversize) never reach it, so the call rate here is accepted requests, not offered load.
panels.title: Input Preparation Latency by Format

panels.description: The segment-merge step only — VAD and diarization are inference and live in the row above, so this is pure host arithmetic and should stay in the microseconds. Per-chunk cost divides it by the chunks produced, which is the number to watch if merging ever stops being free. diarization mode merges within speaker boundaries and so does more work than vad_only.
panels.title: Chunking Latency by Mode

panels.description: Chunk fan-out split by mode, the multiplier on every per-chunk cost downstream: each chunk pays a full 30s encoder frame however short it is. diarization should sit above vad_only because speaker changes force a chunk boundary that duration alone would not. A rise here with flat VAD segment counts means merging is splitting more, not that the audio changed.
panels.title: Chunks per Request by Mode

panels.description: Mean host-side seconds per request for the three stages that run before the device is touched, stacked. All three are observed once per request, so the heights are directly comparable and the total is the fixed latency floor no device speed-up can remove. VAD normally dominates by orders of magnitude; if input preparation ever rivals it, look at the format mix.
panels.title: Host-Side Front-End Cost per Request

title: TT Media Server (Python)
